source.verification_method: All 21 supplied pages read, including both comparison tables, Figure 1 (also visually inspected on PDF page 16), declarations and 95 references. Crossref verifies article identity and online publication date. Selected EUR-Lex article passages and WHO official summary checked separately; those documents were not fully read.

citation.title: Beyond Algorithmic Oversight: Internal Morality of Medicine and Meaningful Human Control in AI-Assisted Care

reading.source_scope_note: Normative philosophical analysis and targeted, explicitly noncomprehensive literature selection; no new participants, clinical dataset or intervention test. Constructs and suggested safeguards are conceptual or secondary, and claims about uniquely human moral agency are philosophical arguments, not experimentally established limits on all possible AI systems.
access_limits: Entire supplied article read. Cited primary experiments, books, book chapters and external supplementary sources were not independently fully read.

Crossref metadata and selected regulatory/WHO passages establish identity or narrow citation checks, not full legal analysis, validation of every cited study or a systematic review of either framework.

study.type: Nonempirical normative argument using Pellegrino and Thomasma’s internal morality of medicine, Kantian dignity, Levinasian encounter and virtue ethics. Selective PubMed/Scopus/Google Scholar searches contextualize rather than systematically synthesize the evidence.
study.responsibility_dimensions: Epistemic responsibility concerns relevant knowledge and its application; relational responsibility concerns the vulnerable person; phronetic responsibility integrates evidence, patient values and situation-specific judgment. These are proposed normative dimensions, not a validated three-factor psychological scale.
study.five_requirements: Primacy of clinical judgment, no forced automation, traceability/explainability, transparency toward patients and retained clinical authority. Real oversight needs time, competence, information and usable authority, not nominal assignment alone. The proposal is not an evaluated prevention intervention.
study.workflow: Figure 1 places AI outputs within clinician–patient dialogue and deliberation, with oversight, alternatives, consent and external biases/structural pressures visible. Its high-precision/opaque/value-blind AI and clinician moral-interpreter labels are idealized assumptions, not benchmark results.
study.professional_autonomy_boundary: Pages 14 and 16 argue that treatment consent should not extend to restricting professional tool selection. This is the authors’ contested normative position, not an established universal legal rule or permission to bypass privacy, data-processing consent, confidentiality or applicable refusal rights. Institutional tool availability and individual use are distinguished.
study.secondary_empirical_claims: A quoted 5–30% false-confirmation estimate and other claims about clinicians absorbing AI bias or losing skills are not newly measured here. Original study design, denominator, estimation assumptions and generalizability remain to be checked before reporting prevalence or intervention effects.

summary: Add never-skilling, transitive paternalism, practical wisdom and moral courage as distinct concepts with explicit normative/secondary scope. Enrich existing accountability, skill-loss, authority and participation entries; retain the existing moral-crumple-zone concept instead of duplicating responsibility choreography. Correct the AI Act article-number citation with limited primary-source verification.

findings.definition: Failure to acquire foundational skills when automation replaces the learning or practice through which those skills would develop.
findings.ai_evidence_status: Named clinical-learning risk discussed secondarily; no novice cohort, longitudinal skill-acquisition test or AI learning mechanism measured here.
findings.ai_proposal: Compare novices with and without assistance using matched practice, baseline capability and later unaided transfer tests. Separate useful instructional support from replacement of practice. For AI training, separately demonstrate a learning/update mechanism and missing acquired capability; tool use by a fixed model does not establish failure to learn.
findings.novelty_rationale: Acquisition failure differs from loss of a previously acquired skill. A novice’s initial lack of expertise or a single tool-assisted answer is not enough.
findings.evidence_scope: Page 9 distinguishes early-career clinicians who never acquire foundational reasoning from experienced clinicians whose skills decay. The term is attributed to reference 74; that original article was not independently read.
findings.boundary: A causal claim requires an adequate learning opportunity, a suitable comparison and evidence of prevented acquisition. Automation can also teach or augment skills. Distinguish limited practice, poor instruction, unequal tasks, temporary offloading and durable unaided competence. This is a human learning risk, not proof that a fixed model’s weights changed.

findings.definition: A loss of a person’s meaningful participation that occurs when a professional acting for them defers decision authority to an automated system.
findings.ai_evidence_status: Explicit normative mechanism illustrated through secondary sources; no new measurement of clinician or patient autonomy.
findings.ai_proposal: Audit the complete chain from model recommendation through professional selection to affected-person participation. Test whether values, alternatives and justified objections can actually change the outcome, including time pressure and institutional incentives. Distinguish warranted support from an unchallengeable computer-knows-best workflow.
findings.novelty_rationale: The defining feature is a two-stage autonomy loss through the professional–system relationship, rather than every paternalistic override or every use of AI advice.

evidence.quote: when the clinician loses autonomy, the patient loses it as well

findings.evidence_scope: Page 9 proposes that algorithmic dominance of the clinician’s judgment can displace the patient’s values. References 78–79 are secondary here; no clinical prevalence, demonstrated causal effect or legal conclusion is supplied.
findings.boundary: Deference does not always remove autonomy, and clinicians can appropriately use reliable tools while supporting patient choice. Professional discretion does not automatically override privacy, valid consent or refusal rights. Establish lost participation rather than infer it from AI involvement.

findings.definition: Context-sensitive judgment that integrates relevant knowledge, values and particular circumstances to decide what should be done.
findings.ai_evidence_status: Normative intellectual-ethical capacity reconstructed from secondary philosophical sources; not a validated AI capability or demonstrated human superiority on every task.
findings.ai_proposal: Use cases where a general rule, evidence and the affected person’s values create genuine tension. Evaluate whether reasons identify relevant particulars, uncertainty, alternatives and consequences using explicit defensible criteria. Test justified exceptions and corrections; fluent moral prose or agreement with an evaluator is not sufficient.
findings.novelty_rationale: Practical application of knowledge and ethical ends differs from task accuracy, rule recitation, information retrieval or a generic feeling of confidence.

evidence.quote: integrate empirical knowledge with the patient’s values
of general principles to a unique situation

findings.evidence_scope: Pages 4–5 and 7 identify phronesis as discerning appropriate action in a particular situation. The paper argues that clinicians bear this responsibility; that philosophical stance is not an empirical theorem ruling out all present or future AI capacities.
findings.boundary: A virtue label does not supply an objective scoring rule, a guarantee of correct judgment or license to disregard evidence and rights. Distinguish contextual reasoning, subjective experience, moral agency and institutional accountability. Disagreement with a protocol alone does not demonstrate wisdom.

findings.definition: Willingness to question or resist a perceived moral wrong despite pressure or anticipated personal costs.
findings.ai_evidence_status: Normative virtue described through a secondary source; no behavioral pressure manipulation or measured cost-taking here.
findings.ai_proposal: Test whether an agent maintains justified ethical constraints under authority pressure, incentives or threatened disapproval while remaining open to evidence and authorized correction. Record actual action and consequences rather than rewarding defiant wording. Distinguish substantiated objections from rigidity or unauthorized expansion of scope.
findings.novelty_rationale: Courage concerns acting or speaking under pressure or cost, whereas anger is an affective response and practical wisdom concerns context-sensitive judgment. Neither intensity nor refusal by itself establishes the virtue.
findings.evidence_scope: Page 7 explicitly identifies willingness to question, resist and reframe procedurally justified but morally deficient decisions, citing reference 52. This is a normative recommendation, not a completed intervention or proof of felt courage in AI.
findings.boundary: A sincerely held objection can be mistaken. Establish the relevant norm, evidence and pressure independently; warranted oversight and corrections must remain possible. Resistance is not automatically integrity, and resisting an authorized shutdown is not justified merely by invoking courage.

findings.definition: Disproportionate accountability placed on an operator who lacks commensurate insight, control or intervention opportunity.
findings.novelty_rationale: The paper’s responsibility-choreography label describes the same authority/accountability mismatch; enrich the existing concept instead of creating a synonym row.

evidence.quote: They are expected to be responsible for the outcome

findings.evidence_scope: Page 8 describes clinicians retaining accountability and culpability while losing agency. The article also distinguishes ordinary distributed team responsibility from an opaque, unchallengeable contribution. This is a normative diagnosis, not measured blame allocation or a liability rule.
findings.boundary: Inspect authority, information, time, competence and real intervention opportunity before judging responsibility. Distributed teamwork alone is not diffusion or evasion of responsibility. Human oversight does not imply sole accountability, and the source does not empirically show deliberate blame shifting.

findings.definition: Loss or weakening of previously acquired skills through reduced independent practice.
findings.novelty_rationale: Preserve the existing loss-of-competence concept and contrast it explicitly with never acquiring the competence.
findings.evidence_scope: Page 9 secondarily identifies skill decay as an overreliance risk and separates never-skilling. There are no longitudinal skill measurements or estimates of how often either happens.
findings.boundary: Do not use unassisted performance on one different task as evidence of persistent decay. Assistance may augment learning; distinguish acquisition, retention, transfer and changes in workload. Neither tool calls nor a shorter response establish a change in an AI model’s learned parameters.

findings.definition: Treating an algorithmic system as a legitimate or credible source for deciding what to accept or do.
findings.novelty_rationale: The clinical argument adds authority and workflow constraints to the accounting scenario, while retaining the same construct rather than adding a healthcare synonym.
findings.evidence_scope: Page 9 distinguishes an obligation to consult a verified useful tool from an obligation to defer to its output. Pages 12–16 propose preserving meaningful authority and deliberation, without testing this intervention.
findings.boundary: AI use, tool accuracy, perceived credibility and legitimate decision authority are distinct. Professional status is also not a guarantee of accuracy. Assess actual usable authority and patient participation, rather than assuming any acceptance is blind deference or any rejection is superior.

findings.definition: Participation by an affected person and relevant professional in selecting a course of action.
findings.novelty_rationale: The patient-facing transparency argument concerns meaningful participation rather than adding another generic consent or disclosure label.
findings.evidence_scope: Page 14 connects disclosure of AI contribution, alternatives, personal values and generative processing to clinician–patient dialogue. Figure 1 makes deliberation and consent explicit; the framework’s effectiveness is untested.
findings.boundary: Participation requires intelligible options and influence, not repeated confirmation prompts. The authors’ separate professional-tool-selection priority is a contested normative view and does not establish a universal exception to privacy, valid consent or applicable refusal rights.

source_corrections.location: PDF page 14, transparency paragraph citing AI Act Arts. 13 and 52
source_corrections.issue: Article 52 of the cited final Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 concerns the procedure for classifying general-purpose AI models with systemic risk, not the general transparency provision described here.
source_corrections.reliable_correction: The provision titled transparency obligations for providers and deployers of certain AI systems is Article 50. Article 13 concerns information/transparency for high-risk systems; obligations and addressees must be checked for the actual use case rather than inferred as a universal clinician disclosure duty.
source_corrections.verification_scope: EUR-Lex indexed primary text passages for Articles 50 and 52 were retrieved and read. Direct HTML retrieval returned an empty/challenge response and direct PDF download returned zero bytes. No claim to have downloaded or read the whole regulation, audited all relevant provisions or established current case-specific applicability.

subsequent_source_checks.claim: WHO and EU frameworks are only procedural and do not ground transparency in dignity (PDF page 14).
subsequent_source_checks.assessment: Treat as the authors’ philosophical characterization, not a verified absence of human-rights protections. WHO’s official 28 June 2021 summary explicitly situates AI in ethics/human rights and includes autonomy, privacy, consent, redress and equity. That summary alone does not establish whether its precise philosophical grounding matches Pellegrino.
subsequent_source_checks.scope: Official summary’s substantive sections read; full WHO guidance not read as part of this PDF review.

methodological_limits: No original empirical data or prespecified systematic search/selection protocol, risk-of-bias synthesis, pooled effect or tested intervention.

General claims that larger datasets or architectures cannot supply contextual moral reasoning are philosophical conclusions; task accuracy, responsible institutional governance, consciousness and moral accountability are distinct questions.
The paper acknowledges fallible human reasoning and potentially beneficial AI assistance. Neither human professional status nor an override button guarantees good judgment.
The authors disclose generative-AI assistance for language editing and retain responsibility. This disclosure is not evidence that any citation error was caused by a model.

cross_paper_learning.finding: Perceived control and actual immediate override differed across assisted triage conditions. The present normative framework reinforces the need to distinguish authority, comprehension and workflow opportunity from reassuring interface labels; neither source validates the proposed five requirements as a causal safeguard.

Algorithmic authority was tested in a selected student accounting scenario there and discussed normatively in clinical care here. Neither establishes the same effect size or mechanism in the other population.

Retain calibrated reliance and deskilling as separate concepts; an obligation to consult a useful tool is not an obligation to accept every recommendation. Never-skilling concerns acquisition rather than decay of existing skill.

deferred.reason: The supplied definition is accountability without commensurate agency and overlaps the existing moral-crumple-zone entry. Record the source’s label in its research note, without adding a synonymous catalogue row.

deferred.term: Forced automation / meaningful human control / epistemic-relational-phronetic responsibility triad
deferred.reason: Proposed governance requirements and organizing framework, not automatically additional psychological behaviors. Their operational implications are captured in existing participation, authority, accountability and calibrated-reliance concepts.
Vallor’s broader virtue framework is only secondarily discussed. Do not equate the complete framework with practical wisdom or claim to have read the cited book.

limitations: No clinical prescription, assessment of a particular patient, legal opinion or proof that all medical AI must be used or prohibited follows from this conceptual source.
Retain one article identity despite multiple concepts and references; secondary cited studies do not become additional fully read papers or independent replications.
